title: Gravity in the Solar System
seo_title: Grade 8 Gravity in the Solar System Worksheets: Orbits, Planets and Galaxies
standard_text: Develop and use a model to describe the role of gravity in the motions within galaxies and the solar system.
meta_desc: Free middle school science worksheets on gravity in the solar system (NGSS MS-ESS1-2): how gravity makes orbits, planet distance and orbital speed data, and gravity's role in forming the solar system and holding galaxies together. 100 practice questions with answers.
key_big: Gravity keeps planets and stars in orbit.
key_sub: Forward motion plus gravity's pull makes an orbit. Closer planets move faster; gravity also holds galaxies together.
body_html:
How to think about it

Gravity controls motion in space. An orbit happens when an object moving forward is pulled toward a larger mass: the pull bends its path into a curve.

  • The Sun has more than 99% of the solar system's mass, so the planets orbit it.
  • Planets closer to the Sun feel a stronger pull, move faster and have shorter years. Farther planets are slower with longer years.
  • Gravity formed the solar system from a collapsing cloud and holds the Milky Way together; the Sun orbits the galaxy's center.
Example

Without the Sun's gravity, how would Earth move?

No force to curve its path.

Answer: in a straight line

Example

Neptune or Mars: which moves faster?

Closer → faster.

Answer: Mars

Common mistakes

  • Thinking a planet would fall into the Sun without gravity. It would fly off straight.
  • Thinking outer planets move faster.
  • Thinking nothing pulls on orbiting planets.

faq.q: Why do planets orbit the Sun?
faq.a: Each planet is moving forward, and the Sun's gravity pulls it inward. Together they bend its path into an orbit.

faq.q: Why do planets farther from the Sun take longer to orbit?
faq.a: They travel a longer path and the Sun's weaker pull at that distance means they move more slowly.

faq.q: What role does gravity play in galaxies?
faq.a: Gravity holds the stars, gas and dust of a galaxy together, and stars like the Sun orbit the galaxy's center.

items.q: Does Earth's gravity reach the Moon?
c: No, it stops at the atmosphere.
Yes. It keeps the Moon in orbit.
items.e: Gravity reaches far into space.

items.q: Chloe asks: “Why do moons orbit planets instead of flying off?”
c: The planet's gravity pulls on the moving moon.
items.e: Same idea at a smaller scale.

items.q: What shape are most planetary orbits?
items.e: Slightly stretched circles.

items.q: Emma asks: “Why does a comet speed up as it gets close to the Sun?”
c: The Sun's gravity pulls harder when the comet is closer.
items.e: Closer → stronger pull → faster.

items.q: Nora asks: “What does the Sun orbit?”
c: the center of the Milky Way galaxy
items.e: One trip takes about 230 million years.

items.q: Why do outer planets take longer to orbit the Sun?
c: They travel a longer path and move more slowly because the Sun's pull is weaker.
items.e: Distance matters.
